title: Shopgirl
full_review:
The breathtaking aerial shots of Los Angeles that open "Shopgirl" (Touchstone) -- an adaptation of Steve Martin's novella -- would seem to portend a glossy old-style romantic film.

It's too bad what follows turns out to be such a languidly paced downer about Mirabelle (an appealing Claire Danes), a lonely salesgirl at Saks looking for love.

An ordinary night at the local laundromat brings about a meeting with nerdy, awkward font artist Jeremy (Jason Schwartzman). Though the scruffy, hirsute lad seems the last person in the world to whom the simple but stylish Mirabelle would be attracted, in her
desperation she agrees to go out on a date with him.

He's completely ill at ease and socially naive, and the evening fizzles, but days later, both on the same wavelength, they meet again and this time she invites him into her bedroom.
The absence of a condom seems to bring the would-be sexual encounter to a halt, but he bums one off a neighbor (much to her embarrassment), and they sleep together.

Soon after this tentative fling, a wealthy older businessman, Ray Porter (Martin), purchases a pair of expensive woman's gloves from her, but much to her surprise sends them to Mirabelle as a gift with a note asking her out to dinner.

After their meal, faster than you can say "check, please," she's lying prone and naked on his bed, and the pair commence a no-strings-attached affair that proves only fitfully satisfying for her. Ray assures colleagues that he's been clear with her about the future, not looking for anything "permanent," while she in turn tells her girlfriends that she believes he really loves her.

The relationship hits a big snag when Ray confesses that he's slept with an old girlfriend. But after a period of estrangement, Mirabelle comes back to him -- encouraged no doubt by the fact that he's paid off her onerous bank loan.

Jeremy, meanwhile, has a growth experience traversing the country with a rock band, and their paths cross, bringing him back into her life.

Director Anand Tucker does his best with this material -- and achieves the intended bittersweet tone -- but somehow it all feels patently unreal.

So, too, there's something a little self-aggrandizing about Martin -- though bravely showing Ray to have unlikable traits -- letting his character off the hook by signaling the audience that he's really just a sad soul who can't help behaving badly.

Danes, as already noted, makes a lovely heroine -- a bit Natalie Wood, a bit Audrey Hepburn -- but Mirabelle pairing with the immature and callow Jeremy is just plain improbable. At least as the film progresses Jeremy cleans up his act and his presence becomes more palatable, and Mirabelle's lingering affection for him slightly more plausible. Perhaps all of this was more believable on the printed page.

Despite a feel-good ending, and (presumably) a morally sound resolution, the ethical choices made by these characters -- all in the name of the story's theme of "the quest to find connection" -- are dubious. Beyond that, strictly as entertainment, "Shopgirl" lacks momentum.

This film contains a smattering of crude language, brief profanity, partial and rear nudity, sexual situations and banter, a permissive view of premarital sex and condom use. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
